title: Neolithic Revolution begins in Mesopotamia
summary: Human beings in Mesopotamia (one of three global sites alongside China and America) began gradually shifting from hunting and gathering to agricultural settlements, marking the start of the Neolithic Revolution.

citation.quote: Starting in 15,000 BCE, for reasons that are still debated, human beings gradually shifted from hunting and gathering ways of life to agricultural settlements.

title: Göbekli Tepe built in North Kurdistan
summary: The oldest known Neolithic edifice, Göbekli Tepe (Xerawreşk) in North Kurdistan, was constructed with massive stone pillars, likely serving as a place of assembly or temple complex.

citation.quote: The oldest known Neolithic edifice is located in North Kurdistan, at Xerawreşk (Göbekli Tepe; in English, Potbelly Hill). Dated at 10,500 BCE, it seems to have been a place of assembly or a temple complex, with massive stone pillars.

title: Strong female goddess figures at Tell Halaf
summary: Female goddess figures typical of the Neolithic age were found at Tell Halaf, dating to 6000 BCE, representing a religious tradition that later gave way to myths of patriarchal domination beginning in the fifth millennium BCE.

citation.quote: Beginning in the fifth millennium BCE, in mythology, the strong female goddesses typical of the Neolithic age (as found on Tell Halaf, dating to 6000 BCE) gave way to myths of patriarchal domination.

title: First large cities emerge in upper Mesopotamia
summary: Urban society emerged in the fourth millennium BCE with large cities such as Tell Brak and Uruk, accompanied by innovations in writing, irrigation, and transportation, giving rise to the earliest states.

citation.quote: Urban society emerged in the fourth millennium BCE with the first large cities such as Tell Brak (in today's Cizîrê canton) and Uruk (in what now is southern Iraq).

title: Serêkaniyê established under the Mitanni empire
summary: The city of Serêkaniyê is said to have been established around 2000 BCE under the ancient Mitanni empire. The city sits on the Turkish border and its northern part is today occupied by Turkey.

citation.quote: The city of Serêkaniyê (Kurdish for "At the Source"; in Arabic, Ra's al-'Ain; in Syriac, Res Ayna) was established in 2000 BCE, it is said, under the Mitanni empire.

title: Syriacs appear in the archaeological record
summary: The Syriac people, who claim descent from the ancient Assyrians, first appear in the archaeological record around 2000 BCE in Mesopotamia.

citation.quote: They claim to be indigenous to Mesopotamia and to descend from the Assyrians, appearing in the archaeological record around 2000 BCE.

title: Sea Peoples arrive and Hittite kingdom collapses
summary: In the eleventh century BCE, the Sea Peoples—described as a melding of peasant rebels and social bandits—arrived from the west, causing the Hittite kingdom to devolve into chaos and creating a power vacuum in present-day Rojava.

citation.quote: in the eleventh century BCE, as the Sea Peoples—apparently a melding of peasant rebels and social bandits—arrived from the west, the Hittite kingdom devolved into chaos.

title: Assyrians subdue Aramaean principalities
summary: In the seventh and eighth centuries BCE, the Assyrians subdued the Aramaean principalities of upper Mesopotamia, though the Aramaean language subsequently became the lingua franca of western Mesopotamia.

citation.quote: In the seventh and eighth centuries BCE, the Assyrians subdued the Aramaean principalities, but the Aramaean language became the lingua franca in western Mesopotamia.

title: Present-day Syria becomes part of the Roman Empire
summary: In 62 BCE, the region of present-day Syria was incorporated into the Roman Empire, beginning a period of Roman rule in the area.

citation.quote: In 62 BCE, the region of present-day Syria became part of the *Imperium Romanum*.

title: Battle of Yarmouk: Arab forces conquer eastern Roman Syria
summary: At the Battle of Yarmouk in 636 CE, Muslim and Arab troops conquered eastern Roman Syria, bringing the region under Islamic rule with the Umayyad caliphs ruling from Damascus.

citation.quote: At the beginning of the Islamic expansion, Muslim/Arab troops conquered eastern Roman Syria at the Battle of Yarmouk in 636 CE, and the Umayyad caliphs ruled the region from Damascus.

title: Abbasids overthrow the Umayyads
summary: In 750 CE, the Abbasid dynasty overthrew the Umayyad caliphs and moved the seat of the caliphate from Damascus to Baghdad.

citation.quote: In 750 CE, the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads and moved the caliphate's seat to Baghdad.

title: Ottoman Empire conquers Syria
summary: In 1516, the Ottoman Empire overran Syria, beginning a period of Ottoman rule over the region that would last, with periodic insurrections, until 1918.

citation.quote: Finally, in 1516, the Ottoman Empire overran Syria. Ottoman rule continued, punctuated by insurrections, until 1918.

title: Paris Commune established as council-based institution
summary: The Paris Commune of 1871 marked the beginning of organization by councils as an integral part of European and Russian socialist movements, with councils serving as its main institutions.

citation.quote: Ever since the Paris Commune of 1871, organization by councils has been an integral part of the European and Russian socialist movements. Councils were the main institutions in the Paris Commune, in the Russian Revolution of 1917, and in the German uprisings of 1918, when workers' and soldiers' councils were established.

title: Lewis H. Morgan publishes Ancient Society
summary: Lewis H. Morgan published Ancient Society, a foundational work on primitive communism and communal social organization that influenced later thinkers including Öcalan.

citation.quote: Lewis H. Morgan, Ancient Society (1877); Friedrich Engels, The Origin of the Family, Private Property, and the State (1894), and V. Gordon Childe, Man Makes Himself (1941).

title: Ottoman defeat in Russo-Turkish War leads to refugee settlement in Syria
summary: After the Ottoman Empire lost the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–78, it settled some war refugees in Syria. These settlers became the ancestors of today's Syrian Turkmens.

citation.quote: In the nineteenth century, after the Ottoman Empire lost the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–78, it settled some of the war refugees in Syria.

title: Circassians settle in the Rojava region
summary: Circassians established a presence in the area by 1878, some resettling from the Balkans and others arriving via the Turkish port city of Samsun and Kayseri before reaching Syrian territory.

citation.quote: Circassians have been in the area since 1878. Some resettled from the Balkans, while others traveled from the Caucasus to the Turkish port city of Samsun, thence to Kayseri and subsequently to Syrian territory.

title: Kobanî city founded as a company town
summary: Kobanî city was established in 1892 as a company town during the construction of the Berlin-Baghdad Railway. Its name is thought to derive from the German word Kompanie (company).

citation.quote: Its capital, Kobanî city, was founded in 1892 as a company town during the construction of the Berlin-Baghdad Railway.

title: Birth of Kurdish intellectual Nurî Dersîmî
summary: Nurî Dersîmî, the Kurdish intellectual after whom the Rojava academies are named, was born in 1893. He advocated for Kurdish cultural and linguistic rights and resisted Ba'ath regime persecution throughout his life.

citation.quote: Nurî Dersîmî (1893–1973) fought for the Kurdish people's rights to their culture and language and never bent under the Ba'ath regime persecution and repression.

title: Friedrich Engels publishes The Origin of the Family, Private Property, and the State
summary: Friedrich Engels published his influential work tracing the origins of patriarchy, the state, and private property, which shaped Marxist understandings of primitive communism.

citation.quote: Lewis H. Morgan, Ancient Society (1877); Friedrich Engels, The Origin of the Family, Private Property, and the State (1894), and V. Gordon Childe, Man Makes Himself (1941).

title: Ottoman Empire launches genocidal campaign against non-Muslim populations
summary: The Ottoman Empire issued a call for jihad against all non-Muslim populations and carried out deportations and massacres that killed 1.5 million Armenians, 750,000 Syriacs, 500,000 Pontic Greeks, and others.

citation.quote: In 1915, to enforce Islamization, the Ottoman Empire issued a call for jihad against all non-Muslim populations within its domains: all non-Turkish populations were to be destroyed. The deportations and massacres that followed cost the lives of 1.5 million Armenians, 750,000 Syriacs, and 500,000 Pontic Greeks, as well as other Christian groups and Ezidis.

title: Deir ez-Zor camp becomes final destination of Armenian death marches
summary: During the Ottoman-perpetrated Armenian genocide, concentration camps were established in the Syrian desert. In 1915, the camp at Deir ez-Zor became the terminal point of the death marches.

citation.quote: Concentration camps were created in the Syrian desert, and in 1915, the camp at Deir ez-Zor became the final destination of the death marches.

title: Sykes-Picot Agreement secretly concluded
summary: Britain and France secretly concluded the Sykes-Picot Agreement, defining their respective colonial spheres of interest and shaping the political divisions of the Middle East for the next century.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: On May 16, 1916, Britain and France secretly concluded the Sykes-Picot Agreement, which defined their respective spheres of colonial interest—and the political divisions of the Middle East for the next century.

title: Russian Revolution organized through councils
summary: Councils were the main institutions of the Russian Revolution of 1917, part of a broader tradition of council-based organization in socialist movements.

citation.quote: Ever since the Paris Commune of 1871, organization by councils has been an integral part of the European and Russian socialist movements. Councils were the main institutions in the Paris Commune, in the Russian Revolution of 1917, and in the German uprisings of 1918, when workers' and soldiers' councils were established.

title: Ottoman Empire collapses at end of World War I
summary: In 1918, the Ottoman Empire—a close German ally—collapsed at the end of World War I, ending Ottoman rule over Syria after four centuries and drawing in Germany, Russia, Britain, and France as competing powers over its remnants.

citation.quote: Ottoman rule continued, punctuated by insurrections, until 1918. The Ottoman Empire, a close German ally, collapsed at the end of World War I.

title: German uprisings establish workers' and soldiers' councils
summary: The German uprisings of 1918 saw the establishment of workers' and soldiers' councils, though the council movement was ultimately defeated by counter-revolution.

citation.quote: Councils were the main institutions in the Paris Commune, in the Russian Revolution of 1917, and in the German uprisings of 1918, when workers' and soldiers' councils were established. But in all cases, the council movement was neutralized, either because the revolution consolidated (in the case of the Soviet Union), or because the counter-revolution defeated it (in the Paris Commune and the German council movement).

title: Hesekê established by the French Mandate
summary: Hesekê was founded in the 1920s and 1930s by the French Mandate administration, initially settled by Syriacs fleeing the Ottoman Empire. By 2011, the city's estimated population was 188,000.

citation.quote: Hesekê, settled by Syriacs fleeing the Ottoman Empire, was established in the 1920s and 1930s by the French Mandate.

title: San Remo conference divides Middle East into mandated territories
summary: The San Remo conference of 1920 divided the Middle East in favor of the colonial powers England and France, redrawing the region into the mandated territories of Syria and Iraq.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: The San Remo conference of 1920 divided the Middle East into parts that favored the interests of the colonial powers England and France, and re-drew the region into the mandated territories of Syria and Iraq.

title: Syria becomes part of the French Mandate; Circassians side against Arab rebels
summary: In 1920, when Syria became part of the French Mandate, Syrian Circassians repeatedly sided against rebellious Arabs, which seriously damaged relations between the two groups.

citation.quote: In 1920, after Syria became part of the French Mandate, the Syrian Circassians repeatedly sided against rebellious Arabs, which seriously damaged relations between the two groups.

title: Colonial powers divide Serêkaniyê along Syrian-Turkish border
summary: The city was split in two when colonial powers drew the Syrian-Turkish border through it, renaming the southern portion Ras Al-Ayn and the northern Turkish part Ceylanpınar.

citation.quote: The city was cut in two in the 1920s, when the colonial powers drew the Syrian-Turkish border through it. The Syrian-occupied southern portion was renamed Ras Al-Ayn and the Turkish northern part was called Ceylanpınar.

title: French Mandate established over Syria
summary: At the outset of the French Mandate in 1921–22, Syria's Arabs were nomads, with no Arab villages yet established in the Cizîrê region.

citation.quote: In 1921–22, at the outset of the French Mandate, Syria's Arabs were nomads. The first Arab village in Cizîrê was not founded until 1933.

title: Artificial Syrian-Turkish border drawn, dividing Kobanî
summary: The artificial Syrian-Turkish border was drawn in 1923, splitting the city of Kobanî; the Turkish border town Mürşitpinar, north of the railroad, had formerly been a suburb of Syrian Kobanî.

citation.quote: The artificial Syrian-Turkish border, drawn in 1923, divided the city: the Turkish border town Mürşitpinar (in Kurdish, Etmenek), north of the railroad, was formerly a suburb of Syrian Kobanî.

title: French Army establishes Qamişlo as administrative center
summary: The French Army founded Qamişlo city in 1926 to serve as an administrative center and military garrison. It also became a home for Christian refugees from Turkey, and many Syriacs still live there today.

citation.quote: The French Army established Qamişlo city in 1926 to serve as an administrative center and military garrison; it also served as a home for Christian refugees from Turkey, and many Syriacs still live there today.

title: Muslim Brotherhood founded in Egypt
summary: The Muslim Brotherhood was founded in Egypt in 1928, combining Islamic law with a social program; it became active in Syria by 1945–46.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: The Muslim Brotherhood, founded in Egypt in 1928, was active in Syria by 1945–46, combining Islamic law with a social program.

title: Syrian Kurds rebel against Arab rule and agitate for autonomy in Cizîrê
summary: In the 1930s, Syrian Kurds rebelled against Arab rule from Damascus and agitated for autonomy in Cizîrê.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: In the 1930s, Syrian Kurds rebelled against Arab rule from Damascus and agitated for autonomy in Cizîrê.

title: First Arab village founded in Cizîrê
summary: The first Arab village in the Cizîrê region was established in 1933, prior to which the area had no Arab villages.

citation.quote: The first Arab village in Cizîrê was not founded until 1933.

title: France adds more regions to Syrian state
summary: Under British pressure, France formed a Syrian state around Damascus and the Aleppo region, and added more regions to it in 1937.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: Under pressure from Britain, France formed a Syrian state around Damascus and in the Aleppo region, adding more regions in 1937.

title: France places Cizîrê under direct colonial control
summary: In response to Kurdish agitation for autonomy, the French government in 1938 placed Cizîrê under its direct control.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: In response, in 1938, the French government placed Cizîrê under its direct control.

title: Ba’ath Party founded in Syria
summary: Syria’s Ba’ath (“Reawakening”) Party was founded in 1940, seeking to stimulate pan-Arabist consciousness; it was secular, anti-imperialist, and offered careers to supporters of Arab nationalism.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: Syria’s Ba‘ath (“Reawakening”) Party, founded in 1940, sought to stimulate pan-Arabist consciousness: it was secular and anti-imperialist, offering careers to supporters of Arab nationalism.

title: V. Gordon Childe publishes Man Makes Himself
summary: V. Gordon Childe published Man Makes Himself, a work on prehistoric human development and the emergence of civilization that contributed to understandings of primitive communism.

citation.quote: Lewis H. Morgan, Ancient Society (1877); Friedrich Engels, The Origin of the Family, Private Property, and the State (1894), and V. Gordon Childe, Man Makes Himself (1941).

title: War between Kurds and Arab tribes in Cizîrê
summary: In 1945 war broke out between Kurds and Arab tribes in the region, during which 150 Kurdish villages were looted.

citation.quote: In 1945, war broke out between Kurds and the Arab tribes, during which 150 Kurdish villages were looted.

title: Last French troops depart Syria
summary: After repeated Allied promises of Syrian independence and sustained pressure from riots, rebellions, and British intervention, the last French troops finally departed the region on April 15, 1946.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: During World War II, the Allies repeatedly promised Syrian independence, but was only under pressure of riots and rebellions and British intervention did the last French troops finally depart the region on April 15, 1946.

title: Independent Republic of Syria declared
summary: Two days after the last French troops departed, the independent Republic of Syria was declared.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: Two days later, the independent Republic of Syria was declared.

title: Syria participates in the Palestine war
summary: In 1948, Syria participated in the Palestine war (Israeli war of independence), in which Israel decisively defeated the Arab states, expelled 750,000 Palestinians, and established the State of Israel—an event known in Arabic as Al-Nakba.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: In 1948, Syria participated in the Palestine war (Israeli war of independence), in which the Israelis decisively defeated the Arab states, expelled 750,000 Palestinians, and established the State of Israel (in what is termed in Arabic  Al-Nakba, “the catastrophe”).

title: Syria endures twenty governments and four constitutions amid military coups
summary: Following defeat in the 1948 Palestine war, Syria descended into political instability; between 1949 and 1956 the country had twenty different governments and four different constitutions amid repeated military coups.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: between 1949 and 1956, Syria had twenty different governments and four different constitutions.

title: Kurdish nationalist El Partî founded in Syria
summary: Kurds excluded from pan-Arabism founded the Kurdish nationalist El Partî in 1957, from which most of the region’s later Kurdish parties would issue.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: others founded the Kurdish nationalist El Partî in 1957, from which would issue most of the region’s later Kurdish parties.

title: KDP-S (Syrian branch of KDP) founded
summary: The KDP-S, the Syrian branch of the South Kurdish KDP led by Abdulhakim Bashar, was founded in 1957 and later came to dominate the ENKS coalition.

citation.quote: Together these three parties make up the KDP-S, the Syrian branch of the South Kurdish KDP (also led by Bashar), founded in 1957.

title: Egypt and Syria declare the United Arab Republic
summary: On February 1, 1958, Egypt and Syria declared a union known as the United Arab Republic (UAR), intended to unite all Arab countries in a pan-Arabist nation with strong central state control.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: On February 1, 1958, Egypt and Syria declared a union known as the United Arab Republic (UAR).

title: Armenian refugees depart Kobanî for Aleppo or Armenia
summary: Most Armenian refugees who had settled in Kobanî, fleeing Ottoman persecution, left in the 1960s for Aleppo or Armenia.

citation.quote: Armenian refugees settled here as well, fleeing persecution by the Ottoman Empire, but most left in the 1960s for Aleppo or Armenia.

title: Arab Belt resettlement program builds villages around Serêkaniyê
summary: Arab villages were built surrounding Serêkaniyê during Syria's Arab Belt resettlement program in the 1960s.

citation.quote: Surrounding the city are Arab villages, built during the Arab Belt resettlement program of the 1960s.

title: Oil drilling begins in Cizîrê
summary: The Ba'ath regime began extracting petroleum in Cizîrê, which held 50–60 percent of Syrian oil production, drilling a heavy grade of crude.

citation.quote: Cizîrê also has oil wealth, constituting 50–60 percent of Syrian oil production. Drilling began in the 1960s, extracting petroleum of a heavy grade.

title: Syrian military declares Syrian Arab Republic, ending the UAR
summary: On September 28, 1961, the Syrian military, supported by the upper classes, declared the Syrian Arab Republic, putting an end to the United Arab Republic.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: On September 28, 1961, the Syrian military, supported by the upper classes, declared the Syrian Arab Republic, putting an end to the UAR.

title: Ba'ath regime distributes land to semi-nomadic farmers in Hesekê
summary: After the Ba'ath Party seized power in 1963, it redistributed large agricultural fields to semi-nomadic stock farmers in the Hesekê region, who then began cultivating grain and cotton. This accompanied the Xabur Project, which built dams and irrigation channels.

citation.quote: After the Ba'ath regime took power in 1963, it distributed huge fields among the semi-nomadic stock farmers there, who began to cultivate grain and cotton.

title: Syria's state of emergency imposed
summary: A state of emergency was imposed in Syria in 1963, remaining in force for nearly five decades until it was finally lifted in June 2011.

citation.quote: In June, the state of emergency that had been in place since 1963 was ended.

title: Kurdish villagers in Derna dispossessed of their land
summary: In 1963, residents of the village of Derna were stripped of their land, which was redistributed to establish new Arab villages, leaving the Kurdish community without land or resources.

citation.quote: "In 1963 we were dispossessed of all this land," Gulinda says. "We didn't have anything anymore. So now only women and children live here. Everyone else went away, much to our sorrow. Almost all the land was redistributed to build new Arab villages."

title: Ba’athist officers carry out coup against Syrian old elites
summary: On March 8, 1963, Ba’athist officers carried out a coup against the old elites, asserting middle-class military careerists who distributed power among themselves and minority clients.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: Then on March 8, 1963, Ba‘athist officers carried out a coup against the old elites.

title: Ba'ath Party decides to establish Arab Belt along Turkish border
summary: In 1965, the Ba'ath Party decided to create a 200-mile Arab Belt along the Turkish border to shift the area's demography from Kurdish to Arab, stretching from Serêkaniyê eastward to the Iraqi border.

citation.quote: In 1965, the Ba'ath Party decided to establish an Arab Belt along the Turkish border, 200 miles (322 kilometers) long and 6–10 miles wide. The purpose was to shift the area's demography from Kurdish to Arab.

title: Coup overthrows traditional Ba’ath leadership; Hafez Al-Assad becomes defense minister
summary: On February 23, 1966, a coup overthrew the traditional Ba’ath leadership with the support of Syrian Air Force General Hafez Al-Assad, who became minister of defense.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: On February 23, 1966, a coup overthrew the traditional Ba‘ath leadership, with the support of Syrian Air Force General Hafez Al-Assad, who became minister of defense.

title: Kurdish armed struggle begins in the 1970s
summary: The Kurdish freedom movement's current round of armed struggle began in the 1970s, eventually evolving through dramatic ideological changes over subsequent decades.

citation.quote: The Kurdish freedom movement has evolved in stunningly dramatic ways since the beginning of the current round of armed struggle in the 1970s.

title: Şarabia tribe settled in Til Hemîs
summary: The Şarabia, one of the largest Arab tribes, settled in Til Hemîs in 1970, establishing themselves in a town that was 80 percent Arab.

citation.quote: But one of the largest aşîret, the Şarabia, who had settled in Til Hemîs in 1970, traditionally clash with the Şammar.

title: Assad seizes power and imprisons former political leadership
summary: On November 16, 1970, Hafez Al-Assad seized power, imprisoned the entire former political leadership, and created a system described as a presidential monarchy.

citation.chapter: Colonialism, Pan-Arabism, and the Ba’ath Party
citation.quote: On November 16, 1970, Assad seized power and threw the entire former political leadership into jail, creating a system that can best be called a presidential monarchy.

title: Syria implements Arabization project under Hafez al-Assad
summary: After Hafez al-Assad became head of state, Syria began implementing the Arabization project in 1973 under the name 'Plan to Build State Model Farms in the Jazirah Region,' constructing 41 Arab villages along the Turkish border and Arabizing all Kurdish place names.

citation.quote: In 1973, after Hafez al-Assad became head of state, Syria began to implement the Arabization project, under the name "Plan to Build State Model Farms in the Jazirah Region."

title: Death of Kurdish intellectual Nurî Dersîmî
summary: Nurî Dersîmî, who spent his life fighting for Kurdish cultural and linguistic rights under Ba'ath regime repression, died in 1973. Academies across Rojava's major cities were later named in his honor.

citation.quote: Nurî Dersîmî (1893–1973) fought for the Kurdish people's rights to their culture and language and never bent under the Ba'ath regime persecution and repression.

title: Leyla Qasim executed in Baghdad
summary: Leyla Qasim, the best-known female Kurdish fighter, was executed in Baghdad in 1974; her portrait hangs in many YPJ institutions today.

citation.chapter: 8.11 The Significance of the YPG and YPJ
citation.quote: The best-known female fighter was Leyla Qasim, who was executed in Baghdad in 1974; her portrait hangs in many YPJ institutions today.

title: Founding of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK)
summary: Abdullah Öcalan, Sakine Cansız, and other Kurdish and Turkish revolutionaries founded the PKK in North Kurdistan as a Marxist-Leninist liberation movement.

citation.chapter: 3.1 The PKK and its Paradigm Shift
citation.quote: In 1978, Kurdish and Turkish revolutionaries, among them Abdullah Öcalan and Sakine Cansız, founded the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) in North Kurdistan as a Marxist-Leninist liberation movement.

title: Sakine Cansız detained as political prisoner
summary: Sakine Cansız was detained as a political prisoner beginning in 1979, remaining imprisoned until 1992, before becoming a leading figure in the PKK women's movement.

citation.chapter: 3.1 The PKK and its Paradigm Shift
citation.quote: Sakine Cansız, detained a political prisoner from 1979 to 1992, subsequently became a leading figure of the PKK women's movement and cofounded the women's army YAJK.

title: Military coup in Turkey
summary: The Turkish military seized power for the third time in the country's history. The coup, carried out in consultation with the United States, led to the arrest of some 650,000 people.

citation.chapter: 3.1 The PKK and its Paradigm Shift
citation.quote: On November 12, 1980, the military seized power in Turkey for the third time. The coup, the most brutal in Turkish history, and carried out in consultation with the United States, would traumatize Turkish society for years to come.

title: Massacre at Hama
summary: The Syrian government carried out a massacre at Hama in 1982, referenced in the chapter as context for the Syrian Muslim Brotherhood's continued commitment to militant Islam.

citation.chapter: 14.1 The Islamization of the Syrian Opposition
citation.quote: Despite the slaughter at Hama in 1982, "the Syrian Muslim Brotherhood stood firmly in the tradition of militant Islam."

title: PKK initiates guerrilla war against the Turkish state
summary: The PKK launched its armed guerrilla campaign against the Turkish state in Turkish-occupied North Kurdistan. Thousands of young Kurds from Syria, men and women alike, joined the guerrilla army.

citation.chapter: 3.1 The PKK and its Paradigm Shift
citation.quote: On August 15, 1984, the PKK initiated a guerrilla war against the Turkish state in Turkish-occupied North Kurdistan.

title: Murray Bookchin publishes The Rise of Urbanization and the Decline of Citizenship
summary: Murray Bookchin published this work critiquing capitalist modernity and urbanization, cited in the chapter as a reference for ecological and communalist critiques of historical materialism.

citation.quote: Murray Bookchin, The Rise of Urbanization and the Decline of Citizenship (San Francisco, CA, 1986).

title: Murray Bookchin publishes The Rise of Urbanization and the Decline of Citizenship
summary: Murray Bookchin's book The Rise of Urbanization and the Decline of Citizenship was published in San Francisco in 1987, articulating the communalist vision of self-governed economic entities as part of a citizen-controlled institutional framework.

citation.quote: Murray Bookchin, *The Rise of Urbanization and the Decline of Citizenship* (San Francisco, CA, 1987), [p. 263].

title: Culture and Art association founded illegally in Rojava
summary: The civil society association Culture and Art (Çand û Hûner) was founded in 1988, long before the revolution, initially operating illegally. It later grew to establish cultural academies across Rojava's cities.

citation.quote: Culture and Art is a civil society association dedicated to advancing culture. Founded in 1988—long before the revolution—it was initially organized illegally.

title: Armenian Apostolic Church opens genocide memorial complex in Deir ez-Zor
summary: The Armenian Apostolic Church opened a memorial complex in Deir ez-Zor to commemorate the victims of the Armenian genocide. The site drew tens of thousands of Armenian visitors annually on April 24, the genocide remembrance day.

citation.quote: In 1989–90, the Armenian Apostolic Church opened a complex in Deir ez-Zor to memorialize this tragedy.

title: Turkey razes Ezidi villages in North Kurdistan
summary: During the 1990s, Turkey destroyed Ezidi villages in North Kurdistan while the German Federal Republic, which hosted around 100,000 Ezidi refugees, looked the other way.

citation.quote: yet when Turkey razed Ezidi villages in the 1990s, the Federal Republic turned a blind eye.

title: Collapse of the Soviet Union ends Real Socialism
summary: The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1990–91 brought Real Socialism to an end, causing liberation movements worldwide to disintegrate and prompting the PKK to search for alternative political models.

citation.chapter: 3.1 The PKK and its Paradigm Shift
citation.quote: In 1990–91, with the collapse of the Soviet Union, Real Socialism came to an end. Liberation movements around the world disintegrated. The end of Real Socialism led to a searching critique of statism, and in the early 1990s, the PKK began pondering other models.

title: First peace committees formed in Kurdish-majority Syrian cities
summary: In the 1990s, under the Ba'ath regime, activists in Syrian cities with Kurdish majorities formed the first peace committees, which ran clandestinely parallel to the state justice system.

citation.chapter: 9. The New Justice System Consensus Is Key
citation.quote: In the 1990s, under the Ba'ath regime, activists in Syrian cities with Kurdish majorities formed the first peace committees. The state considered them a threat to its monopolistic justice system, so they ran clandestinely, parallel to the existing system.

title: Turkish state destroys over 4,000 Kurdish villages and displaces millions
summary: In the 1990s, Turkish state forces destroyed more than 4,000 rural villages, expelled up to 3 million residents, and murdered more than 17,000 civilians in North Kurdistan.

citation.quote: In the 1990s, state forces destroyed more than 4,000 rural villages and expelled up to 3 million residents, murdering more than 17,000 civilians.

title: Women fought in Peshmerga ranks during uprisings against Ba'ath regime in Iraq
summary: In the uprisings against Iraq's Ba'ath regime before 1991, a few women fought in the ranks of the Peshmerga, a historical precedent noted in contrast to the later combat exclusion of women by the Peshmerga.

citation.chapter: 8.11 The Significance of the YPG and YPJ
citation.quote: In Iraq, in the uprisings against the Ba'ath regime before 1991, a few women fought in the ranks of the Peshmerga

title: PKK creates YAJK, the women's army of Kurdistan
summary: The PKK established the YAJK (Union of Free Women of Kurdistan) as an autonomous women's army with its own headquarters. The YAJK developed principles of autonomous women's organizing, dual leadership, and a minimum 40 percent women's participation in all areas.

citation.chapter: 3.1 The PKK and its Paradigm Shift
citation.quote: In 1993, the PKK created a women's army known as YAJK (the Union of Free Women of Kurdistan), with its own headquarters.

title: Kurdish women decide to establish a women's army
summary: In 1993, Kurdish women made the decision to establish a dedicated women's army, a step that few believed possible at the time but that grew into a regular armed force.

citation.quote: Back in 1993, when Kurdish women decided to establish a women's army, only a few really believed such a thing was possible. Today, as a regular army, they are successfully doing battle with IS.

title: Öcalan proposes Kurdish-language instruction in private homes in Rojava
summary: Abdullah Öcalan, then living in Syria, proposed that the Kurdish language be taught in private homes. In many places in Rojava, the proposal was taken up.

citation.quote: Rojava's Kurdish education movement originated, Berîvan explains, in 1993, when Abdullah Öcalan, then living in Syria, proposed that the Kurdish language be taught in private homes.

title: Gurbetelli Ersöz arrested and Kurdish newspaper Özgür Gündem banned
summary: Gurbetelli Ersöz, editor-in-chief of the Kurdish newspaper Özgür Gündem in Turkey, was arrested on December 10, 1993, and the paper was banned. She was released after six months but proceedings against her continued and she could no longer find work as a journalist.

citation.quote: She was arrested on December 10, 1993, and the paper was banned. After six months, she was released, but the proceedings against her continued, and she could no longer find work as a journalist.

title: KDP and PUK militias war against each other in South Kurdistan
summary: In South Kurdistan, the two major parties—the KDP and the PUK—had militias that actively warred against each other from 1994 to 1998, cited as a cautionary example against a second Kurdish military force in Rojava.

citation.chapter: 6.5 The Supreme Kurdish Council (SKC)—Desteya Bilind a Kurd
citation.quote: a second military force would lead to intra-Kurdish conflicts, as in South Kurdistan, where the two parties, the KDP and the PUK, had militias that actively warred against each other from 1994 to 1998.

title: Gurbetelli Ersöz joins PKK guerrilla army
summary: In 1995, Gurbetelli Ersöz, former editor-in-chief of the Kurdish newspaper Özgür Gündem who had been barred from journalism after her arrest, joined the PKK guerrilla army.

citation.quote: In 1995, she joined the PKK guerrilla army.

title: Syrian oil production reaches its peak
summary: By 1995, Syrian oil production hit its peak; thereafter reserves shrank and output slowly declined.

citation.quote: By 1995, Syrian production reached its peak. Since then, its reserves have shrunk, and oil production has slowly but surely decreased.

title: Diyar Dêrîk killed in fighting with KDP in Gare
summary: Diyar Dêrîk, brother of Kurdish activist Heval Amer and a courier, was killed in 1997 during a war with the KDP in Gare, in the Medya Defense Zones of South Kurdistan.

citation.quote: His brother, Diyar Dêrîk, a courier, was killed in 1997 in a war with the KDP in Gare (in South Kurdistan, in the Medya Defense Zones).

title: Gurbetelli Ersöz killed in KDP ambush
summary: On October 7, 1997, Gurbetelli Ersöz lost her life in an ambush by the KDP. The date was later adopted by RAJIN Rojava as the annual day commemorating women journalists in Kurdistan.

citation.quote: On October 7, 1997, she lost her life in an ambush by the KDP.

title: Turkish and Syrian officials secretly meet at Ceyhan
summary: Turkish and Syrian officials met secretly in the Turkish city of Ceyhan, where Syria agreed to expel the PKK. Assad subsequently shut down all PKK camps and forced Öcalan to leave Syria.

citation.chapter: 3.1 The PKK and its Paradigm Shift
citation.quote: On October 20, 1998, Turkish and Syrian officials secretly met in the Turkish city of Ceyhan. Syria promised to break up the PKK camps and expel them, and as a result, Assad shut down all the PKK camps and forced Öcalan to leave Syria.

title: PKK institutions in Syria collapse after Öcalan's abduction
summary: Following the abduction of Abdullah Öcalan in 1999, PKK institutions in Syria collapsed. Many fighters with a Rojava background later returned and joined the YPG when the revolution began in 2012.

citation.quote: After the abduction of Abdullah Öcalan in 1999, PKK institutions in Syria had collapsed, but now many fighters with a Rojava background came back and joined the YPG (as the defense force had been renamed).

title: Syrian state's intensified repression disrupts Kurdish-language instruction in Rojava
summary: After 1999, Syrian state repression intensified and disrupted Kurdish-language instruction, forcing it underground — small groups of ten or fifteen teachers and students meeting secretly in rotating homes.

citation.quote: The Syrian state's intensified repression after 1999 disrupted Kurdish-language instruction, but it continued surreptitiously—ten or fifteen teachers and students would meet, each time in a different home to avoid detection.

title: Emancipatory school system established in Maxmur refugee camp
summary: In the Maxmur (Makhmur) refugee camp in South Kurdistan, beyond the reach of the KDP and PUK, a school system was established where Kurmancî — the dialect spoken in Rojava — was taught to around 12,000 North Kurdish refugees.

citation.quote: Meanwhile, in the late 1990s, in the refugee camp in Maxmur (Makhmur) in South Kurdistan, a specific school system was established beyond the reach of the KDP and PUK.

title: Qamişlo's garbage pits dug despite known danger to water supply
summary: Qamişlo's garbage pits were dug in 1999, even though the potential danger to drinking water was already known, with water wells located less than a kilometer from the dumpsite.

citation.quote: Qamişlo's garbage pits were dug in 1999, even though the potential danger was known.

title: Öcalan arrested and abducted from Nairobi
summary: Abdullah Öcalan was arrested and abducted by the CIA, and probably indirectly the Mossad, from the Greek consulate in Nairobi, Kenya, and brought to Turkey.

citation.chapter: 3.1 The PKK and its Paradigm Shift
citation.quote: On February 15, 1999, Öcalan was arrested and abducted. The CIA—and probably indirectly the Mossad—abducted him from the Greek consulate in Nairobi, Kenya, and brought him to Turkey.

title: Iraq War triggers mass displacement of Iraqi Christians
summary: According to Syriac Union Party head Ishan Gawriye, Iraq's Christian population collapsed from 14.5 million before the 2003 Iraq War to only 400,000, with none remaining in Baghdad.

citation.quote: "In Iraq, there were previously 14.5 million Christians before the 2003 Iraq War. Now there are only 400,000, and none live in Baghdad anymore."

title: PYD (Democratic Union Party) founded in Syria
summary: The Party of Democratic Unity (PYD) was founded in 2003, building on clandestine committee and working group organizing that Kurdish movement activists in Rojava had been conducting before that date.

citation.quote: Even before the Party of Democratic Unity (PYD) was founded in 2003, Kurdish movement activists in Rojava were creating committees and working groups clandestinely.

title: Abu Musab Al-Zarqawi founds Jama'at al-Tawhid wal-Jihad
summary: Jordanian militant Abu Musab Al-Zarqawi founded Jama'at al-Tawhid wal-Jihad (Monotheism and Jihad) in August 2003, targeting coalition forces and Iraqi Shiites.

citation.quote: In August 2003, the Jordanian Abu Musab Al-Zarqawi founded a group—Jama'at al-Tawhid wal-Jihad (Monotheism and Jihad)—that targeted the coalition forces as well as Iraqi Shiites.

title: Serhildan uprising in Qamişlo
summary: The serhildan (uprising) in Qamişlo in 2004 represented the nadir of Kurdish-Arab relations, with several Arab tribes allied with the Ba'ath regime attacking Kurds, who fought back.

citation.quote: the nadir of Kurdish-Arab relations was the serhildan (uprising) in Qamişlo in 2004, in which several Arab tribes allied with the Ba'ath regime to attack Kurds, and Kurds fought back.

title: Osman Öcalan attempts to split the PKK
summary: In 2004, Osman Öcalan participated in an attempt to split the PKK and tried to reorient the organization along nationalistic-neoliberal lines; when he failed, he left and took many members with him.

citation.quote: In 2004, he participated in an attempt to split the organization. During the ideological transformation, Osman Öcalan tried to reorient it along nationalistic-neoliberal lines. When he failed, he left, taking many members with him.

title: Syrian military helicopters bomb Kurdish areas in Dêrîk region
summary: During operations around Girziro, Syrian military helicopters bombed Kurdish areas, an event recalled by Heval Amer as a precedent when the same occurred during the 2012 liberation.

citation.chapter: 4.6 The Liberation of Dêrîk and Afrîn
citation.quote: Military helicopters arrived, and as in 2004, we were bombed.

title: Increased repression of Kurdish peace committees after 2004
summary: After 2000 and especially after 2004, the Ba'ath regime intensified repression of Kurdish peace committees, yet they continued to operate in smaller numbers and limited areas.

citation.chapter: 9. The New Justice System Consensus Is Key
citation.quote: Even with the increased repression after 2000 and especially after 2004, however, they continued to operate, albeit in smaller numbers and limited areas.

title: Qamişlo soccer riot: Arab Ba'athists attack Kurdish fans
summary: At a soccer match in Qamişlo between a Kurdish team and an Arab team, armed Ba'athists bused in with official approval attacked Kurdish fans with iron chains and weapons, triggering a broader uprising that left an estimated 70 dead.

citation.quote: On March 12, 2004, in Qamişlo, a soccer game was to be held between the Kurdish team Al-Cihad from Qamişlo and the Al-Fatwa team from Deir ez-Zor.

title: Şîlan Kobanî and three PYD cadres killed near Mosul
summary: Senior PYD leader Şîlan Kobanî (Meysa Bakî), a member of both the PYD and Kongra Gel leadership, was killed near Mosul along with three other leading party cadres.

citation.quote: on November 29, 2004, Şîlan Kobanî and three other leading cadres of the PYD were killed near Mosul

title: Şehîd Şîlan Kobanî killed in attack on Mosul
summary: PYD leader Şehîd Şîlan Kobanî (also known as Meysa Bakî) was killed in an attack on Mosul. The three women's military academies in Rojava's cantons were later named in her honor.

citation.quote: Each of the three cantons has a women's military academy, named after Şehîd Şîlan Kobanî (also known as Meysa Bakî), a PYD leader who was killed in an attack on Mosul on November 29, 2004.

title: Iraqi Constitution creates Kurdistan Regional Government
summary: The Iraqi Constitution of 2005 formally established the Kurdistan Regional Government as the official governing body of the predominantly Kurdish region of northern Iraq.

citation.chapter: Prologue: On the Road to Til Koçer
citation.quote: The KRG was created by the Iraqi Constitution of 2005 and is governed by the Democratic Party of Kurdistan (KDP).

title: Rafiq Al-Hariri assassinated, Syrian officials blamed
summary: Lebanese politician Rafiq Al-Hariri was murdered in 2005, with high-ranking Syrian functionaries blamed, leading to Syria's international isolation and its strategic partnership with Turkey against the Kurds.

citation.quote: Meanwhile in 2005 the Lebanese politician Rafiq Al-Hariri was murdered, and high-ranking Syrian functionaries were blamed.

title: Women found Yekîtiya Star in Rojava
summary: In 2005, women founded Yekîtiya Star, conducting educational sessions, meetings, and grassroots organizing work underground while facing severe repression.

citation.quote: "In 2005 women founded Yekîtiya Star," said Hisên. "They conducted educational sessions, held meetings, and did grassroots work."

title: Democratic Confederalism paradigm announced emphasizing ecology
summary: The Kurdish freedom movement announced a new paradigm in 2005 that placed ecology alongside democracy and gender equality as foundational principles of Democratic Confederalism.

citation.quote: The paradigm announced in 2005 emphasized ecology as much as democracy and gender equality.

title: Mutayibeen Coalition founded; Islamic State of Iraq proclaimed
summary: In October 2006, Al-Qaeda in Iraq joined with Sunni tribes and other insurgents to form the Mutayibeen Coalition, which then proclaimed itself the Islamic State of Iraq.

citation.quote: In October 2006, Al-Qaeda in Iraq teamed up with several Sunni tribes and other insurgents and founded the Mutayibeen Coalition, who then proclaimed themselves the Islamic State of Iraq (ISI; in Arabic, Al-dawla al-Islamija fi-l-Iraq).

title: First divorce obtained by a woman in Syrian-occupied Kurdistan
summary: A TEV-DEM representative recounted that in 2007 she was among the first women in Syrian-occupied Kurdistan to obtain a divorce, illustrating the entrenched patriarchal constraints Kurdish women faced.

citation.quote: In 2007, she was one of the first women in Syrian-occupied Kurdistan to obtain a divorce.

title: DTK begins establishing people's councils in North Kurdistan
summary: Since 2007, the Democratic Society Congress (DTK) had been setting up people's councils in mainly Kurdish areas of Turkey (North Kurdistan), providing a practical model for the PYD's later organizing in Syria.

citation.quote: Since 2007, the Democratic Society Congress (DTK) had been setting up people's councils in the mainly Kurdish areas.

title: Arab activist Aysa Afendi arrested and imprisoned in Aleppo
summary: Arab woman Aysa Afendi was arrested in 2008 for political work, taken to Aleppo, and imprisoned for a year during which she was repeatedly tortured.

citation.quote: In 2008, recalled an Arab woman, Aysa Afendi, "I was arrested because of my political work and taken to Aleppo. There I was imprisoned for a year and tortured repeatedly."

title: Kurds begin establishing Democratic Autonomy in North Kurdistan
summary: At least since 2009, Kurdish communities began implementing neighborhood, district, women's, ecology, and youth councils to establish Democratic Autonomy in many cities, with women's liberation built into the council system.

citation.quote: Meanwhile at least since 2009, Kurds have worked to establish Democratic Autonomy in North Kurdistan. They implemented neighborhood councils, district councils, women's councils, ecology councils, youth councils, and others, creating Democratic Autonomy in many cities.

title: DTP wins majorities in most Kurdish municipalities
summary: In March 2009, the Democratic Society Party (DTP) won majorities in most Kurdish municipalities in Turkey, marking a significant electoral advance for the Kurdish freedom movement.

citation.quote: In March 2009, the Democratic Society Party (DTP) won majorities in most Kurdish municipalities.

title: US embassy cable reveals ENKS leader passed information to CIA and Syrian intelligence
summary: A WikiLeaks-published US embassy cable from November 2009 revealed that ENKS leader Abdulhakim Bashar had passed information to both the CIA and Syrian intelligence services.

citation.quote: US embassy in Damascus to Secretary of State, "No Dividend on SARG-Kurdish Backchannel Talks," WikiLeaks, November 25, 2009.

title: Abdullah Öcalan publishes Jenseits von Staat, Macht und Gewalt
summary: Abdullah Öcalan published this work outlining his theory of democratic confederalism, including his critique of state power and hierarchy as forced impositions rather than inevitable developments.

citation.quote: Abdullah Öcalan, Jenseits von Staat, Macht und Gewalt (Neuss, 2010), [p. 32].

title: Arab Spring uprisings in Tunisia and Egypt
summary: Popular uprisings challenged ruling dictatorships in Tunisia and Egypt, as opposition groups campaigned for democratic transformation and inspired opposition movements across the region.

citation.quote: In late 2010 and early 2011, popular uprisings challenged the ruling dictatorships in Tunisia and Egypt, as opposition groups campaigned for a democratic transformation.

title: Abdullah Öcalan publishes Jenseits von Staat, Macht, und Gewalt
summary: Öcalan's book Jenseits von Staat, Macht, und Gewalt was published in Neuss in 2010, addressing the political economy of Kurdistan and the Middle East.

citation.quote: Abdullah Öcalan, *Jenseits von Staat, Macht, und Gewalt* (Neuss, 2010), [p. 268].

title: Abu Bakr Al-Baghdadi takes over leadership of ISI
summary: In 2010, Iraqi Abu Bakr Al-Baghdadi assumed leadership of the Islamic State of Iraq, the precursor organization to IS.

citation.quote: In 2010, Abu Bakr Al-Baghdadi, an Iraqi, took over the leadership.

title: Kurdish freedom movement declares aim of Democratic Confederalism
summary: The Kurdish freedom movement declared its aim to build a society around Democratic Confederalism, with few observers paying attention at the time.

citation.quote: So in the spring of 2011, when the Kurdish freedom movement declared its aim to build a society around a concept called "Democratic Confederalism," few noticed.

title: Syrian civil war onset triggers mass refugee influx into Afrîn
summary: At the onset of the Syrian civil war, Afrîn canton's population was estimated at 400,000. Refugees fleeing Aleppo then poured into the canton, boosting the population to 1.2 million.

citation.quote: At the onset of the Syrian civil war in 2011, the canton's population was estimated at 400,000, but once the attacks began, many refugees from Aleppo immigrated to Afrîn, boosting the population to 1.2 million.

title: Syrian war begins, accelerating Armenian emigration from Rojava
summary: When the Syrian war began in 2011, many Armenians fled to Hesekê province and then to Armenia, compounding a decline already underway from two decades of Arabization policy.

citation.quote: Even before the Syrian war began in 2011, Syria's Armenian population had declined after twenty years of the Arabization policy. According to the Syriac National Council, once the war began, many Armenians fled to Hesekê province and then to Armenia.

title: Women's academies and educational centers open in Rojava
summary: Since 2011, two women's academies and 26 educational centers have opened across Rojava, serving Kurdish cities, villages, and Arab cities with large Kurdish populations.

citation.chapter: Women’s Education and Research Centers—Navenda Perwerde û Zanist Jinê
citation.quote: Since 2011, two women’s academies have opened, as well as 26 educational centers.

title: Yekîtiya Star begins building women's ideological academies
summary: Since 2011, Yekîtiya Star has been establishing academies aimed at strengthening women ideologically, drawing on Jineolojî—the science of women developed by PKK guerrilla fighters.

citation.chapter: Women’s Education and Research Centers—Navenda Perwerde û Zanist Jinê
citation.quote: Since 2011, Yekîtiya Star has been building academies whose purpose is to strengthen women ideologically.

title: Rojava council system constituted as parallel structure to the state
summary: By 2011, the PYD's council system was sufficiently developed to constitute a vibrant structure parallel to the Syrian state, allowing Kurds to pursue a 'third way' without armed confrontation with either the Assad regime or the Islamist opposition.

citation.quote: Nonetheless, in 2011, the council system was sufficient to constitute a vibrant structure parallel to the state without being in direct conflict with it.

title: Economics commissions focus on food supply in their first two years
summary: During 2011–13, the MGRK economics commissions were primarily occupied with ensuring the food supply for the population of Rojava.

citation.quote: During their first two years (2011–13), the economics commissions were occupied mainly with the food supply.

title: National Coordination Body for a Democratic Change initiated in Syria
summary: The National Coordination Body for a Democratic Change was initiated in Syria in 2011 but remained ineffective within the country. Many of its members later became involved in the Syrian Democratic Council (MDS).

citation.quote: Many members of the MDS were previously engaged in the National Coordination Body for a Democratic Change, which was initiated in 2011 but remained ineffective within Syria.

title: YXG mixed-gender defense force founded in Rojava
summary: The YXG was founded in 2011 as a mixed-gender force, with two out of three members of the general command being women, though initially only a few women joined.

citation.quote: When the YXG was founded in 2011, it was a mixed-gender force—two out of three members of the general command were women.

title: Abdullah Öcalan publishes Democratic Confederalism
summary: Abdullah Öcalan's text Democratic Confederalism was published in 2011, outlining the theoretical basis for self-government and an alternative economic system oriented toward societal needs.

citation.quote: Abdullah Öcalan, *Democratic Confederalism* (2011), [p. 21], http://bit.ly/1AUntIO.

title: Jabhat Al-Nusra founded in Syria
summary: Abu Mohammed al-Jaulani, a Syrian loyal to Al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri, formed Jabhat Al-Nusra li-Ahli ash-Sham. Together with thirteen Salafist groups, it strove to establish a radical Islamic emirate in Syria.

citation.quote: Jabhat Al-Nusra li-Ahli ash-Sham (Support Front for the People of Syria) was formed by Abu Mohammed al-Jaulani, a Syrian loyal to the Al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri in late 2011.

title: Ahrar Al-Sham emerges as major Syrian opposition group
summary: Ahrar Al-Sham (Islamic Movement of the Free Men of the Levant) emerged in 2011 as one of the largest opposition groups in Syria, affiliated with Al-Qaeda and supported by Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar.

citation.quote: Ahrar Al-Sham (Islamic Movement of the Free Men of the Levant), which emerged in 2011, is one of the largest opposition groups in Syria.

title: BDP gains electoral success in Turkey
summary: In 2011, the BDP, successor to the banned DTP, achieved electoral success, continuing the Kurdish movement's growing parliamentary presence despite Turkey's 10 percent threshold.

citation.quote: In 2011, the successor party, called the BDP, gained electoral success as well.

title: National Coordination Body (NCC) created in Syria
summary: The Kurdish freedom movement advocated a peaceful democratic solution for Syria from the time of the NCC's founding in the summer of 2011.

citation.quote: The Kurdish freedom movement, as we have seen, has its own ideas about the future of Syria, having advocated a peaceful democratic solution ever since the creation of the NCC in the summer of 2011.

title: Mass arrests of Kurdish activists in Aleppo
summary: In a single week in February 2011, approximately one hundred people were arrested in Aleppo as the Assad regime intensified repression of Kurdish political organizing.

citation.quote: In one week in February 2011 a hundred people were arrested in Aleppo.

title: First Syrian protests held in several cities
summary: The first Syrian protests took place in February 2011 in several cities, though they were small and had limited impact.

citation.quote: The first Syrian protests were held in February 2011 in several cities, but they were small and had limited impact.

title: Dara'a protests erupt after arrest and torture of youths
summary: In mid-March 2011 in Dara'a, police arrested two youths who had sprayed slogans on a wall; one was reportedly fatally tortured in custody. Strong protests demanding their release and political reform broke out, police opened fire killing several demonstrators, and unrest spread across Syria.

citation.quote: Then in mid-March in Dara'a, in the south, two youths had allegedly sprayed slogans on a wall. Syrian police arrested them, and some sources report that while in custody, one youth was fatally tortured.

title: Syrian uprising begins; PYD decides to create people's councils
summary: Once the Syrian uprising began in March 2011, the PYD foresaw a long and brutal conflict and made a conscious decision to create people's councils across Rojava and other Kurdish-populated areas of Syria as institutions of self-rule independent of party structures.

citation.quote: Once the Syrian uprising began in March 2011, the PYD foresaw that a long and brutal conflict could develop. So it made a conscious decision to create a set of people's councils, both in Rojava and in other parts of Syria where it had strong, supportive Kurdish populations.

title: Kurdish activists establish peace committees across neighborhoods after Syrian uprising
summary: After the Syrian uprising began in March 2011, Kurdish activists established peace committees in great numbers at the neighborhood and village community levels.

citation.chapter: 9. The New Justice System Consensus Is Key
citation.quote: It was because of the long experience of these peace committees that, after the Syrian uprising began in March 2011, Kurdish activists were able to establish them in great numbers at the neighborhood and village community levels.

title: Kurdish openly taught in Rojava after March 2011
summary: After March 2011, it became possible to teach Kurdish openly in Rojava. Eleven teachers from the Maxmur camp spent a year doing so.

citation.quote: After March 2011, it became possible to teach Kurdish openly in Rojava, and eleven teachers from the Maxmur camp spent a year doing so.

title: Syria announces stateless Kurds will receive citizenship
summary: In April 2011, a Syrian ministry announced that stateless Kurds — the ajanib registered as 'foreigners' — would finally receive Syrian citizenship. Many Kurdish activists saw this as an attempt to induce Kurdish support for the regime.

citation.quote: And in April, a Syrian ministry announced that the stateless Kurds would finally receive Syrian citizenship, and the next month they were told they had the right to work.

title: Syrian Kurds told they have the right to work
summary: The month after the citizenship announcement, in May 2011, Syrian Kurds were told they had the right to work. The concessions applied only to the ajanib — those registered as 'foreigners' — not to the unregistered maktoumeen.

citation.quote: And in April, a Syrian ministry announced that the stateless Kurds would finally receive Syrian citizenship, and the next month they were told they had the right to work.

title: Syria's state of emergency lifted after 48 years
summary: In June 2011, Syria ended the state of emergency that had been continuously in place since 1963, one of the concessions won by the protest movement during the Arab Spring.

citation.quote: In June, the state of emergency that had been in place since 1963 was ended.

title: Free Syrian Army founded by former soldiers
summary: In July 2011, former soldiers led by onetime Colonel Riad Al-Asaad founded the Free Syrian Army as the armed wing of the Syrian opposition. Comprising mainly Sunnis, it received financial backing from the Gulf States and support from Turkey.

citation.quote: In July, former soldiers, including onetime Colonel Riad Al-Asaad, founded the Free Syrian Army (FSA) as the armed wing of the Syrian opposition. It comprised mainly Sunnis, who were Syria's majority. The Gulf States backed the FSA financially.

title: People's Council of West Kurdistan (MGRK) established
summary: About three hundred delegates from Rojava and other parts of Syria met to establish the MGRK, electing a 33-person coordinating body called TEV-DEM to develop people's councils, commissions, and coordinating bodies.

citation.chapter: 6.2 The People’s Council of West Kurdistan (MGRK)—Meclîsa Gela Rojavayê Kurdistan
citation.quote: By August 2011, perhaps almost half of Rojava’s Kurds were organized in councils. That month, about three hundred delegates from Rojava and other organized parts of Syria met to establish the People’s Council of West Kurdistan (MGRK) to further develop people’s councils, commissions, and coordinating bodies.

title: MGRK holds its first meeting and elects the TEV-DEM for all of Rojava
summary: The People's Council of West Kurdistan (MGRK) convened for the first time in August 2011, electing a TEV-DEM of 33 people to represent all of Rojava, excluding Aleppo.

citation.quote: When the MGRK met in August 2011 for the first time, it elected the TEV-DEM for all of Rojava, consisting of 33 people (not including Aleppo).

title: Syrian National Council founded in Istanbul
summary: The Syrian National Council (SNC) was founded as an alternative government to the Ba'ath regime, meeting in Istanbul with backing from Turkey, NATO, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar. It was dominated by the Muslim Brotherhood.

citation.chapter: 14.1 The Islamization of the Syrian Opposition
citation.quote: The Syrian National Council (SNC) was founded on August 23, 2011, as an alternative government to the Ba'ath regime. Meeting in Istanbul, it was a product chiefly of Turkey, with support from NATO (including Turkey), Saudi Arabia, and Qatar.

title: Kurdish National Council in Syria (ENKS) formed
summary: About 16 small Kurdish groups in Syria coalesced into a coalition called the Kurdish National Council in Syria (ENKS), forming a counterweight to the MGRK in the Kurdish region.

citation.quote: in October 2011 about 16 small, fractious groups formed a coalition called the Kurdish National Council in Syria (ENKS, Encûmena Niştimanî ya Kurdî li Sûriyê).

title: Armed gangs attack village in Til Temir area
summary: Armed gangs attacked the village of YPJ fighter Jîn in Til Temir in October 2011, killing a relative of hers. The attack prompted her to join the armed resistance despite her parents' objections.

citation.quote: "The gangs attacked our village in October 2011," she says. "A relative of mine was killed. I wanted to study, but when the revolution began, I wanted to join."

title: SNC officially founded in Tunis/Gammarth
summary: The Syrian National Council held its official founding in Tunis/Gammarth, following its unofficial founding on August 23, 2011.

citation.chapter: 14.1 The Islamization of the Syrian Opposition
citation.quote: The SNC was founded unofficially on that date; its official founding was in Tunis/Gammarth on December 18, 2011.

title: Abdullah Öcalan's essay on democratic confederal organization published in Demokratik Ulus Çözümü
summary: Öcalan's essay "Demokratik Konfederal Örgütleme ve Demokratik Özerklik" was published in the collection Demokratik Ulus Çözümü, articulating the principle that power is not to be conquered but an alternative constructed.

citation.quote: Abdullah Öcalan, "Demokratik Konfederal Örgütleme ve Demokratik Özerklik," in Fırat Sezgin, ed., Demokratik Ulus Çözümü (Neuss, 2012) [p. 32].

title: MGRK creates commune level in cities' council structure
summary: With hundreds of thousands flooding neighborhood meetings, the MGRK added a new council tier—the commune at the residential street level—to allow all residents to organize and participate directly.

citation.chapter: 6.2 The People’s Council of West Kurdistan (MGRK)—Meclîsa Gela Rojavayê Kurdistan
citation.quote: By the spring of 2012, hundreds of thousands of people were flocking to the neighborhood meetings, eager to participate, in numbers far greater than the venues could accommodate. So to allow all residents to represent and organize themselves, the MGRK created a new level in the cities’ council structure: the commune, at the level of the residential street.

title: Rojava revolution makes ethnic inclusion a leading MGRK imperative
summary: With the 2012 revolution, bringing in diverse ethnicities and cultures became one of the MGRK's leading imperatives, leading to an active policy of inclusion of Arabs and Chaldeans.

citation.quote: But with the 2012 revolution, bringing in the diverse ethnicities and cultures became one of the MGRK's leading imperatives.

title: FSA and regime forces fire on Kurdish neighborhoods of Aleppo
summary: In spring 2012, fighters of the Ba'ath regime and the FSA began shooting randomly into the Kurdish neighborhoods of Aşrafiye and Şêx Maqsûd, injuring and killing residents. The councils responded by arming youth through the council system and creating YPG units.

citation.quote: But in the spring of 2012, fighters of the Ba'ath regime or the FSA took to shooting randomly, with no warning, into the Kurdish neighborhoods, injuring or killing people. The residents began to arm some of the youth through the council system, creating YPG units, but they weren't trained systematically or professionally and weren't able to cope with the attacks.

title: Asayîş internal security force formed in Aleppo
summary: In fall 2012, the Asayîş was established to handle internal security matters including criminality, violence against women, and extreme alcoholism. Chosen by the councils and accountable to the Aleppo people's council, it was kept organizationally separate from the YPG.

citation.quote: Then in the fall of 2012, the Asayîş [see [9.4]] was formed, to handle internal security matters like criminality, violence against women, and extreme alcoholism. Their numbers were smaller, and they were chosen by the councils and held accountable to the Aleppo people's council.

title: Kurds flee to Aşrafiye and Şêx Maqsûd as the two neighborhoods become Aleppo's safest zones
summary: From summer 2012 through spring 2013, Kurds and even Aleppo's elites sent family members into the two Kurdish neighborhoods, which were considered the most secure areas in a city ravaged by war.

citation.quote: From the summer of 2012 to the spring of 2013, Kurds fled to the two neighborhoods for safety. "Even the city's elites sent their family members into the Kurdish neighborhoods," said Mahmud, "because they were the most secure. Mainly women and children came."

title: Severe hardship in Aleppo's Kurdish neighborhoods under food and fuel embargo
summary: The winter of 2012–13 brought extreme hardship to Aşrafiye and Şêx Maqsûd, with the state cutting electricity, imposing a de facto food embargo, and scarcity of diesel leading to days without bread. Residents burned plastic and wood for heat.

citation.quote: "The state shut down the electricity, and finding food and provisions became harder. There was a de facto food embargo. … Sugar was five times more expensive than before. Sometimes due to the scarcity of diesel, there was no bread. Once there was no bread for five days. The winter of 2012–13 was very hard. For heat, we burned everything, plastic and wood."

title: Revolutionary Youth campaign clears trash from liberated areas of Qamişlo and Hesekê
summary: After state sanitation trucks stopped collecting garbage in liberated areas, trash piled up in streets. The Revolutionary Youth organized a campaign with broad popular support that cleared the accumulated garbage within days.

citation.chapter: Attack on the Qamişlo City Hall
citation.quote: In the fall of 2012, in Qamişlo and Hesekê, trash removal became a problem. The sanitation trucks of the state-controlled municipal administration no longer collected garbage in the liberated areas, so within a few weeks mounds of trash were piling up in the streets.

title: Severe heating crisis strikes Rojava as diesel and heating oil run out
summary: The harsh winter of 2012–13 brought dire heating shortages as Rojava's new administration had little diesel or heating oil in reserve; smuggled fuel was insufficient, prices soared, and residents resorted to burning wood and felling trees.

citation.chapter: Attack on the Qamişlo City Hall
citation.quote: Scarcely was the garbage problem solved than the harsh winter of 2012–13 arrived, bringing dire heating problems. Rojava's heating system depends on oil, of which Cizîrê had plenty, but it had no petroleum refineries—for decades, more than half of Cizîrê's petroleum had been sent to the West Syrian city of Homs for refining.

title: Rojava liberation and onset of acute security threats
summary: Following the liberation of Rojava in 2012, the region came under acute threat from multiple armed groups, making self-defense a critical priority for YPG forces.

citation.quote: Self-defense became critical after the liberation of 2012, when, as YPG spokesman Redur Xelîl recalled, Rojava came under acute threat from several sides: "As long as the regime and other armed groups didn't attack us, we didn't attack anyone."

title: MGRK assigns language schools to dedicated buildings in Rojava
summary: In early 2012, the MGRK assigned language schools to specific buildings, converting even stables into classrooms to meet demand. Classes were attended by people of all ages.

citation.quote: In early 2012, the MGRK assigned language schools to specific buildings: "We even transformed stables into schools, if we had no other options."

title: Many areas of Cizîrê liberated in fall 2012
summary: Many areas of Cizîrê canton were not liberated until the fall of 2012, which contributed to weaker Kurdish-language instruction there compared to Afrîn and Kobanî.

citation.quote: In addition, many areas of Cizîrê were not liberated until the fall of 2012.

title: First hard winter after liberation — flour scarce despite grain surplus
summary: During the first hard winter of 2012–13, grain was plentiful but flour was scarce due to the lack of flour mills, raising the threat of famine in Rojava.

citation.quote: But during that first hard winter of 2012–13, though grain was plentiful, flour—due to the lack of flour mills—was scarce.

title: Turkey closes border crossings to Rojava after 2012 liberation
summary: Soon after Rojava's 2012 liberation, Turkey closed all its border crossings to trade with the cantons, initiating an embargo that severely restricted access to goods.

citation.quote: Soon after the 2012 liberation, Turkey closed all its border crossings to trade.

title: Enforced lower energy consumption in Rojava due to conflict
summary: In 2012, conflict in Rojava caused an enforced reduction in energy consumption, which the authors suggest should be treated as a lesson for adopting permanent new policies rather than restoring pre-revolutionary energy levels.

citation.quote: Lessons can be drawn from the enforced lower energy consumption that occurred in 2012, due to conflict.

title: Long-predicted water shortages become reality in Rojava
summary: In 2012–13, water shortages that had long been anticipated materialized across the Cizîrê and Kobanî regions, with rivers like the Xabur flowing only during winter months and other waterways running dry for much of the year.

citation.quote: In 2012–13, long-predicted water shortages became a reality.

title: Garbage goes uncollected in Qamişlo after liberation
summary: Following the withdrawal of Syrian state administrators to state-controlled neighborhoods, garbage in most Qamişlo neighborhoods lay uncollected for several months during the fall and winter of 2012–13.

citation.quote: The Syrian state's administrators retreated to the state-controlled neighborhoods, with the result that in the fall and winter of 2012–13, the garbage in most Qamişlo neighborhoods lay uncollected.

title: US designates Al-Nusra a foreign terrorist organization
summary: An international public outcry forced the United States to add Al-Nusra to the State Department's list of foreign terrorist organizations. The Syrian opposition, including NC president Ahmad Moaz Al-Khatib Al-Hasani, protested strenuously.

citation.quote: In 2012, an international public outcry forced the United States to put Al-Nusra on the State Department's list of foreign terrorist organizations, which it had hesitated to do.

title: Jaish Al-Islam founded as Liwa Al-Islam by Zahran Alloush
summary: Jaish Al-Islam was founded in 2012 under the name Liwa Al-Islam by Zahran Alloush, son of a Syrian sheikh in Saudi exile, before being renamed in 2013.

citation.quote: Jaish Al-Islam (Army of Islam) was founded in 2012 under the name Liwa Al-Islam by Zahran Alloush, the son of a Syrian sheikh in Saudi exile. It was renamed in 2013, and is particularly strong in southern Syria.

title: Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) founded in Turkey
summary: In 2012, the HDP was established to unite emancipatory forces across Turkey and create a unified opposition, allied with the Democratic Regions Party (DBP) organizing locally in North Kurdistan.

citation.quote: In 2012, the establishment of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) was founded in order to connect emancipatory forces throughout Turkey to represent and to create a unified opposition.

title: Aleppo councils cancel Newroz celebration due to state bombardment
summary: In March 2012, the Aleppo councils decided not to celebrate Newroz, the Iranian new year usually commemorated on March 20–21, because the state was bombarding all public gatherings.

citation.quote: In March 2012, the councils decided not to celebrate Newroz, the old Iranian new year and spring festival usually commemorated on March 20–21, because the state was bombarding all gatherings.

title: Bassam Ishak leads failed SNC reform effort
summary: Bassam Ishak, a Syriac member of the SNC, led a reform effort to broaden representation within the council, but the attempt failed, resulting in only token minority representation while Islamist elements continued to dominate.

citation.chapter: 14.1 The Islamization of the Syrian Opposition
citation.quote: In June 2012, Bassam Ishak, a Syriac member of the SNC, led an effort to reform it to bring in "the whole range of identities in Syria and the whole spectrum of revolutionary forces."

title: Yekîtiya Star economics commission votes to establish women's cooperatives
summary: In Qamişlo, Yekîtiya Star's economics commission met and decided to create a women's economics commission in every city to support the founding of women's cooperatives across Rojava.

citation.quote: On June 10, 2012, in Qamişlo, Yekîtiya Star's economics commission convened and decided to establish a women's economics commission in every city, to support the founding of women's cooperatives.

title: Popular uprisings liberate cities and villages of Rojava from Ba'ath dictatorship
summary: Popular uprisings liberated the cities and villages of Rojava, mostly populated by Kurds, from the Ba'ath dictatorship, establishing a democratic system.

citation.quote: Few noticed either, in July 2012, when popular uprisings, one by one, liberated the cities and villages of Rojava, which are mostly populated by Kurds, from the Ba'ath dictatorship and established a democratic system.

title: American journalists from Vice News encounter YPG checkpoints around Kobanî
summary: A week after the Kobanî liberation, a team of American journalists from Vice News attempting to enter the city were stopped at YPG checkpoints. Armed fighters explained they were preventing FSA forces and statist saboteurs from entering.

citation.quote: A week after the Kobanî liberation, a team of American journalists from Vice News who tried to enter encountered YPG checkpoints. Kobanî "is surrounded by Kurdish checkpoints," they recounted.

title: FSA attacks Aleppo; YPG establishes roadblocks around Kurdish neighborhoods
summary: In July 2012, FSA and armed opposition forces simultaneously attacked Damascus and Aleppo, seizing several neighborhoods. Armed YPG units responded by setting up roadblocks at all entry points to the Kurdish neighborhoods, halting the FSA advance.

citation.quote: But in July 2012, the situation changed almost overnight as the FSA and other armed opposition forces attacked Damascus and Aleppo simultaneously. Rebels from nearby rural areas invaded several neighborhoods, mainly Sunni Arab ones, and took control. In the next days and weeks, armed YPG set up roadblocks at all entry points into Aşrafiye, Şêx Maqsûd, Midan, and Hayderiye and posted guards.

title: July 2012 revolution transforms YXG into YPG
summary: The July 2012 revolution in Rojava led to the transformation of the YXG into the YPG, with thousands more women joining the defense forces.

citation.quote: With the July 2012 revolution and the transformation of the YXG into the YPG, thousands more women streamed in.

title: Rojava revolution renders Syrian justice system obsolete
summary: The July 2012 revolution in Rojava led the people to reject not only the Ba'ath regime's security apparatus but also the existing judicial system and its personnel.

citation.chapter: 9. The New Justice System Consensus Is Key
citation.quote: The revolution in July 2012 rendered the Syrian justice system obsolete. The people, and the political movement behind them, clearly rejected not only the Ba'ath regime, with its state security apparatus, officialdom, and intelligence agencies, but also, and less visibly, the judicial system and its personnel.

title: Peace committees extended to residential street level in Rojava
